Now let Pharaoh appoint overseers throughout the land of Egypt, and let them store food in every city during the years of abundance. It will provide food for the seven years of famine, so that the land will not perish because of the famine, for it will be very severe.
God gave Joseph favor and mercy in Pharaoh's eyes. Pharaoh said to his servants, “We cannot find a man as wise and understanding as this man, for the Spirit of God is with him.”
He appointed him second in command over his whole kingdom, made him ruler over all Egypt, and had him ride in Pharaoh's second chariot.
He clothed him in fine linen and placed a gold chain around his neck.
Joseph ruled over the whole land of Egypt. All Pharaoh's officials, all his servants, and everyone who performed the king's work loved him.

The land of Egypt was at peace before Pharaoh because of Joseph, for God was with him and gave him favor and mercy above all his relatives, before everyone who knew him and those who heard reports about him. Pharaoh's kingdom was well established, and there was no adversary and no evil.
The king gave Joseph the name Zaphenath-paneah.
On the day Joseph stood before Pharaoh, he was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh.

In that year Isaac died. What Joseph had said concerning the interpretation of the two dreams came to pass just as he had told him. There were seven years of abundance throughout the land of Egypt, and the land produced plentifully: one measure yielded eighteen hundred measures.
Joseph gathered food in each city for that city, until they were filled with grain, so much that they could no longer count or measure it because of its abundance.
In the forty-fifth jubilee, in the second week, in the second year, Judah took a wife for Er, his firstborn, from the daughters of Aram. Her name was Tamar.

He hated her and did not sleep with her, because his mother was one of the daughters of Canaan, and he wanted to take a wife for himself from his mother's clan. But his father Judah would not allow him.
Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked, and the Lord killed him.
Judah said to Onan, his brother, “Go in to your brother's wife, perform your duty as her brother-in-law, and raise up offspring for your brother.”
Onan knew that the offspring would not be his but his brother's.
Judah said to Tamar, his daughter-in-law, “Stay as a widow in your father's house until my son Shelah grows up, and I will give you to him as his wife.”
He grew up, but Bedsuel, Judah’s wife, did not allow her son Shelah to marry.
In his sixth year, Judah went up to Timnah to shear his sheep.
She put aside her widow’s clothes, put on a veil, adorned herself, and sat at the gate facing the road to Timnah.
As Judah was traveling, he found her and thought she was a prostitute. He said to her, “Let me come in to you.” She said to him, “Come in,” and he went in.
She said to him, “Give me my payment.” He said to her, “I have nothing with me except the ring on my finger, my necklace, and the staff in my hand.”
She said to him, “Give me those until you send me my payment.”
Judah went to his sheep, and she went to her father's house.

Judah sent a young goat by his Adullamite shepherd, but he failed to find her. He asked the people of the place, “Where is the prostitute who was here?” They said to him, “There is no prostitute here, and we have no prostitute among us.” 15 He returned and told him that he had failed to find her. He said to him, “I also asked the people of the place, and they told me, ‘There is no prostitute here.’”
When three months had passed, it became known that she was pregnant.
Judah went to her father’s house and said to her father and her brothers, “Bring her out and burn her, because she has committed an impurity in Israel.”
When they brought her out to burn her, she sent the ring, the necklace, and the staff to her father-in-law and said, “Recognize whose these are, for I am pregnant by their owner.”
Judah recognized them and said, “Tamar is more righteous than I am. Do not burn her, then.”
For this reason she was not given to Shelah, and he did not approach her again.
After this she conceived and gave birth to two sons, Perez and Zerah, in the seventh year of this second week.
After this, the seven years of abundance that Joseph had told Pharaoh about came to an end.

Judah realized that he had done an evil deed by sleeping with his daughter-in-law, and it was abhorrent in his own eyes. He realized that he had sinned and gone astray, because he had uncovered his son’s nakedness. He began to lament and plead before the Lord because of his sin.
We told him in a dream that he would be forgiven, because he had pleaded earnestly, lamented, and did not do it again.
He received forgiveness because he turned away from his sin and his ignorance, for the offense against our God was great.

You too must command the Israelites that there be no impurity among them, because anyone who sleeps with his daughter-in-law or his mother-in-law has committed an impurity. They must burn with fire both the man who slept with her and the woman, so that wrath and punishment may be removed from Israel.
We told Judah that neither of his two sons had slept with her.
For he went in innocence in his own eyes and sought judgment, because Judah wished to burn her with fire according to the judgment of Abraham, which he had commanded his children.
In the first year of the third week of the forty-fifth jubilee, famine began to come upon the land. Rain was withheld from the land, for none fell. 2 The land suffered famine.
The Egyptians came to Joseph so that he would give them food. He opened the storehouses containing the wheat from the first year and sold it to the people of the land for gold.
Jacob heard that there was food in Egypt, and he sent ten of his sons to obtain food for him in Egypt, but he did not send Benjamin.
Joseph recognized [?], but they did not recognize him.
After this he released them, kept Simeon alone, and sent away his nine brothers. 7 He filled their sacks with wheat and also put their gold into their sacks without their knowing.
He commanded them to bring their youngest brother, because they had told him that their father and their youngest brother were alive.

They went up from the land of Egypt and reached the land of Canaan. They told their father everything that had happened to them, how the ruler of the land had spoken harshly to them, and how he had detained Simeon until they brought Benjamin to him.
Jacob said, “You have made me childless! Joseph is gone, Simeon is gone, and you are taking Benjamin away. Your evil has fallen upon me!”
He said, “My son will not go with you, in case he becomes ill.”
For he saw that all their gold had been returned, each in his own sack, and because of this he was afraid to send him.
The famine increased and grew severe in the land of Canaan and in every land except the land of Egypt.
And he supplied the people of Egypt with food in the first year of the famine.

When Israel saw that the famine had become very severe in the land and there was no escape, he said to his sons, “Go back and get food for us so that we do not die.” 16 They said, “We will not go unless our youngest brother comes with us. We will not go.” 17 Israel saw that unless he sent him with them, they would all perish from the famine.
Reuben said, “Entrust him to my hands. If I do not bring him back to you, kill my two sons in exchange for his life.”
Judah came forward and said, “Send him with us. If I do not bring him back to you, I will bear the guilt before you all the days of my life.”

And he sent him with them in the second year of this week of years, at the new moon. They reached the land of Egypt with all those who were traveling, and he put gifts into their hands: storax resin, almonds, terebinth nuts, and pure honey.
They arrived and stood before Joseph. He saw his brother Benjamin and recognized him. He said to them, “Is this your youngest brother?” They said to him, “He is.”
He sent him into his house, and he also brought Simeon out to them.
They ate before him, and he gave portions to them all. Benjamin’s portion was seven times greater than the portions of all the others.
They ate and drank, then got up and spent the night beside their donkeys.
Joseph devised a plan by which he could discover their thoughts, whether they had peaceful intentions toward one another.
He did as Joseph had told him. He filled all their sacks with food and put their gold into their sacks as well. He put the cup into Benjamin’s sack.

They left early in the morning. When they had gone out from there, Joseph said to the man in charge of his household, “Run after them and confront them, saying, ‘You have repaid me with evil for good. You have stolen from me the silver cup from which my master drinks.’ Bring their youngest brother back to me. Bring him quickly, before I go out to sit in judgment.”
He ran after them.
They said to him, “Far be it from your servants! They would not do such a thing, nor would they steal any possession from your master’s house.”
“How, then, could we steal any possession?”
He said to them, “Not so. Only the man with whom I find it will I take as a slave. The rest of you may return home in peace.”

As he searched through their belongings, he began with the oldest and finished with the youngest. It was found in Benjamin’s sack. 8 They tore their clothes, loaded their donkeys, and returned to the city. They reached Joseph’s house and all bowed down before him with their faces to the ground.

Joseph said to them, “You have done evil.” They said, “What can we say? How can we defend ourselves? Our lord has discovered the guilt of his servants. Here we are, slaves to our lord, along with our donkeys.”

And Joseph said to them, “I fear God. As for you, go to your homes, but let your brother remain a slave, because you have done wrong. Do you not know that a man practices divination with his cup, as I do with this cup? Yet you stole it from me.”
Judah said, “Let the blame fall on me, my lord. Let your servant speak a word in my lord’s hearing.”
“When we go to your servant, our father, and the young man is not with us, he will die. We will cause our father to suffer grief until he dies.”
“Let me alone, your servant, serve as a slave to my lord in place of the boy.”
And Joseph saw that all their hearts were united with one another for good. He could no longer restrain himself and told them that he was Joseph.
He spoke with them in the Hebrew language.
He said to them, “Do not weep over me. Hurry and bring my father here to me so that I may see him before I die. The eyes of my brother Benjamin also see.”
“For this is now the second year of the famine, and there are still five years to come, with no harvest, no fruit on the trees, and no plowing.”
Come down quickly, you and your households. Do not be consumed by the famine, and do not grieve over your possessions, for God arranged to send me ahead of you so that many people might live.
Tell my father that I am still alive. You yourselves now see that God has made me like a father to Pharaoh, a ruler in his house and over the whole land of Egypt.
Tell my father about all my glory and all the wealth and honor God has given me.
At Pharaoh’s command, he gave them wagons and provisions for the journey. He gave all of them colored garments and silver.
He also sent their father garments and silver, and ten donkeys carrying wheat. Then he sent them away.
They went up and told their father.
Their father did not believe them, for he was stunned in his mind.

Israel set out from Haran, from his house, at the beginning of the third month. He went by the road to the Well of the Oath and offered a sacrifice to the God of his father Isaac on the seventh day of that month.
And Jacob remembered the dream he had seen at Bethel and was afraid to go down to Egypt. 3 And he was considering sending word to Joseph to come to him, so that he himself would not have to go down.

He celebrated the harvest festival of the firstfruits of wheat with old wheat, for throughout the land of Canaan there was not even a handful of seed in the ground. There was famine for all the wild animals, livestock, birds, and people.
On the sixteenth day, God appeared to him and said to him, “Jacob, Jacob!” He said, “Here I am.”
“I will go down with you, and I will bring you away. You will be buried in this land, and Joseph will place his hands upon your eyes. Do not be afraid; go down to Egypt.”

His sons and his grandsons rose and loaded their father and their possessions onto the wagons. 8. Israel set out from the Well of the Oath on the sixteenth day of this third month and went to the land of Egypt.
And Israel sent his son Judah ahead of him to his son Joseph to inspect the land of Goshen, because Joseph had told his brothers to come and settle there, so that they would be near him.
It was good land in Egypt and close to him, for everyone and also for the livestock.
These are the names of Jacob’s sons who went into Egypt with their father Jacob. 12. Reuben, Israel’s firstborn, and these are the names of his sons: Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi—five.
Simeon and his sons, and these are the names of his sons: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Saul, the son of a Phoenician woman—seven.
Levi and his sons—and these are the names of his sons: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari—four in all.
Judah and his sons, and these are the names of his sons: Shelah, Perez, and Zerah—four.
Issachar and his sons, and these are the names of his sons: Tola, Puvah, Jashub, and Shimron—five.
Zebulun and his sons, and these are the names of his sons: Sered, Elon, and Jahleel—four.
These are Jacob’s sons and their sons, whom Leah bore to Jacob in Mesopotamia: six, and one sister, Dinah.
The sons of Zilpah, the maidservant of Leah, Jacob’s wife, whom she bore to Jacob, were Gad and Asher.
These are the names of their sons who entered Egypt with him. The sons of Gad: Ziphion, Haggi, Shuni, Ezbon, [Eri], Areli, and Arodi—eight.
The sons of Asher: Imnah, Ishvah, [Juel], and Beriah, and their one sister Serah—five.
There were fourteen people in all, and all those belonging to Leah numbered forty-four.
The sons of Rachel, Jacob’s wife, were Joseph and Benjamin.
And before his father entered Egypt, sons were born to Joseph in Egypt, whom Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, the priest of Heliopolis, bore to him: Manasseh and Ephraim.
The sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, Ashbel, Guad, Naaman, Abihud, Rosh, Sananim, Huppim, and Gaam—eleven.
All the people descended from Rachel numbered fourteen.
The children of Bilhah, the maidservant of Rachel, Jacob’s wife, whom she bore to Jacob, were Dan and Naphtali.
These are the names of their children who entered Egypt with them: the sons of Dan were Hushim, Samon, Asudi, Ijaka, and Solomon—six.
They died in Egypt in the year they entered it, and Hushim alone remained to Dan.
These are the names of the sons of Naphtali: Jahzeel, Guni, Jezer, Shallum, and Iv.
And Ew, who was born after the year of famine, died in Egypt.
All those descended from Rachel numbered twenty-six.
All the people belonging to Jacob who entered Egypt numbered seventy people.
In the land of Canaan, Judah’s two sons, Er and Onan, died without children. The children of Israel buried those who had perished, and they were counted among the seventy people.
Israel entered the country of Egypt, into the land of Goshen, on the first day of the fourth month, in the second year of the third week of years of the forty-fifth jubilee.
And Joseph came to meet his father Jacob in the land of Goshen. He embraced his father's neck and wept.

Israel said to Joseph, “Now I can die, since I have seen you. And now blessed be the Lord, the God of Israel, the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, who has not withheld his mercy and kindness from his servant Jacob.
It is a great thing for me to have seen your face while I am still alive, for the vision I saw at Bethel has truly come to pass. Blessed be the Lord my God forever and ever, and blessed be his name.”
Joseph and his brothers ate bread and drank wine before their father, and Jacob rejoiced with very great joy.
Joseph gave his father and his brothers property so that they could settle in the land of Goshen and in Rameses, and all its districts were theirs to govern under Pharaoh.
Joseph provided for his father, his brothers, and their livestock there, giving them enough for the seven years of famine.
The land of Egypt suffered because of the famine.
The years of famine came to an end.
For during the seven years of famine.
That year was the first year of the fourth week of years of the forty-fifth jubilee.
Joseph took a fifth of the grain they sowed for the king, and left them four parts for food and seed. Joseph established this as a law for the land of Egypt, which remains to this day.
And Israel lived in the land of Egypt for seventeen years.

Before he died, Israel blessed his children and told them everything that would happen to them in the land of Egypt. He made known to them what would come upon them in the latter days, and blessed them.

And he rested with his ancestors and was buried in the cave of Machpelah in the land of Canaan, near his father Abraham, in the grave he had dug for himself in the cave of Machpelah in the land of Hebron.
And he gave all his books and the books of his ancestors to his son Levi, so that he would preserve them and make new copies of them for his children, down to this day.

And after Jacob died, the children of Israel multiplied in the land of Egypt and became a numerous people. They were all united in their hearts, so that each brother loved his brothers and each man helped his brother. They multiplied and increased greatly.
And there was no Satan and nothing evil throughout all the days of Joseph's life that he lived after his father Jacob.
And Joseph died at the age of one hundred and ten years. He had lived in the land of Canaan for seventeen years and had lived as a slave for ten years.
He died, along with all his brothers and that entire generation. 5 Before he died, he commanded the children of Israel to take his bones away when they left the land of Egypt.
And he made them swear an oath concerning his bones, because he knew that the Egyptians would not allow him to be taken out and buried in the land of Canaan at that time.

And he could not enter, because another, new king ruled over Egypt and was stronger than he was. He entered the land of Canaan, and the gates of Egypt were shut. No one went out, and no one entered Egypt.
And Joseph died in the forty-sixth jubilee, in the second year of the sixth week of years. They buried him in the land of Egypt, and all his brothers died after him.
And the king of Egypt went out to fight against the king of Canaan in the forty-seventh jubilee, in the second year of the second week of years.
And many returned to Egypt, while a few of them remained in the hill country of Hebron. Your father Abram remained with them.
And the king of Canaan defeated the king of Egypt and shut the gates of Egypt.
He devised an evil plan against the children of Israel, to oppress them, and said to the people of Egypt:

“Look, the people of the children of Israel have become greater and more numerous than we are. Come, let us deal shrewdly with them before they become more numerous, and let us oppress them with slavery before war comes upon us and they fight against us. Otherwise they will join the enemy and leave our land, for their hearts and faces are turned toward the land of Canaan.”
He appointed taskmasters over them to oppress them with slavery.
They subjected them to harsh slavery, but the more cruelly they treated them, the more numerous they became and the more they increased.
And the people of Egypt treated the children of Israel as unclean.

In the seventh week, in the seventh year of the forty-seventh jubilee, your father came from the land of Canaan. You were born in the fourth week, in its sixth year, in the forty-eighth jubilee, during the days of distress for the children of Israel.
Pharaoh, the king of Egypt, issued a command against them that they should throw all their newborn male children into the river.
They continued throwing them in for seven months, until the day you were born.
And she made a basket for you and coated it with pitch and bitumen. She placed it among the reeds at the riverbank and put you inside it for seven days.

In those days, Pharaoh’s daughter Thermutis went out to bathe in the river. She heard your voice as you were crying and told her Hebrew women to bring you. They brought you to her, and she took you out of the basket and had compassion on you.
Your sister said to her, “Shall I go and call one of the Hebrew women for you, to care for this child and nurse him for you?”
She went and called your mother, Jochebed. She gave her wages, and she brought you up.

After this, when you grew older, they took you to Pharaoh’s house, and you became her son. Your father, [?], taught you writing. When you had completed three weeks of years, he brought you into the royal court.
You remained in the court for three weeks of years, until the day you left the royal court.

On the second day, you found two of the children of Israel fighting. You said to the one who was acting aggressively, “Why are you striking your brother?” He became furious and angry and said, “Who appointed you ruler and judge over us? Do you intend to kill me as you killed the Egyptian?” You became afraid and fled because of this matter.

And in the sixth year of the third week of years of the forty-ninth jubilee, you went and lived there for five weeks of years and one year. You returned to Egypt in the second year of the second week of years of the fiftieth jubilee.
You know what he said to you on Mount Sinai, and what Prince Mastema intended to do to you at the lodging place on the way when you were returning to Egypt.
Did he not seek with all his power to kill you and rescue the Egyptians from your hand? For he saw that you had been sent to carry out judgment and vengeance against the Egyptians.
But I rescued you from his hand.

The Lord carried out great vengeance against them on behalf of Israel. He struck and killed them with blood, frogs, gnats, dog flies, and terrible sores that broke out in blisters; and he struck their livestock with death and hailstones.
And everything was sent [?] your hand, so that you would do what had not been done, and you were to tell it to the king of Egypt, before all his messengers and before his people.
Everything happened at your word. Ten great and severe judgments came upon the land of Egypt, so that you might exact vengeance there for Israel.
And the Lord did everything for the sake of Israel.
Prince Mastema stood before you in opposition to you and wanted to make you fall into Pharaoh’s hands. He helped the Egyptians’ sorcerers, and they opposed you and performed their works before you.
We allowed them to do evil, but we did not allow healing to be performed by their hands.
The Lord struck them with terrible sores, and they were unable to stand against you, because we prevented them from performing even a single sign.

Despite all the signs and wonders, Prince Mastema was not ashamed, until he grew strong and cried out to the Egyptians to pursue you with all their forces, with their chariots and horses, and with the entire multitude of the people of Egypt.
I stood between you, the Egyptians, and Israel, and we rescued Israel from his hand and from the hand of the people.

All the people whom he brought out pursued Israel. The Lord our God threw them into the middle of the sea, into the depths of the abyss beneath the children of Israel. Just as the Egyptians had thrown their children into the river, he exacted vengeance on them a millionfold.
On the fourteenth, fifteenth, sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth days, Prince Mastema was bound and shut away from the Israelites, so that he would not accuse them.
On the nineteenth day, we released them so that they might help the Egyptians and pursue the children of Israel.
He strengthened their [?] and made them strong, and they were strengthened by the Lord our God, so that he might strike the Egyptians and throw them into the middle of the sea.

On the fourteenth day, we bound him so that he would not accuse the children of Israel on the day when they were asking the Egyptians for possessions and clothing—articles of silver, gold, and bronze—and so that they might plunder the Egyptians in return for the forced service they had imposed on them.
We did not bring the children of Israel out of Egypt empty-handed.

Remember the command that the Lord gave you concerning the Passover: you are to observe it at its appointed time, on the fourteenth day of the first month. You are to slaughter it before evening, and they are to eat it at night, on the evening of the fifteenth, from the time the sun sets. For on this night—the beginning of the festival and the beginning of rejoicing—you were sitting and eating the Passover in Egypt.

And this is what the Lord gave them: in every house where they saw the blood of a year-old lamb on its doorway, they were not to enter the house to kill, but were to pass over it, so that everyone in the house would be saved because of the sign of blood on its doorway.

And the Lord’s powers did everything that the Lord had commanded them. They passed over all the children of Israel, and no plague came upon them to destroy any living being among them, from livestock to people, or even a dog.

And the plague in Egypt was very great. There was no house in Egypt without a corpse inside it, and weeping and wailing. 6 And all Israel sat eating the Passover meat and drinking wine, praising, blessing, and thanking the Lord, the God of their fathers, and preparing to leave the yoke of Egypt and its cruel servitude.

You too must remember this day all the days of your life. Observe it from year to year, all the days of your life, once a year on its appointed day, according to all its laws. Do not move it from one day to another or from one month to another. 8 For it is an everlasting ordinance, engraved on the heavenly tablets for the children of Israel, that they should observe it every year on its appointed day, once a year throughout all their generations. There is no limit to its days, for it is ordained forever.

If a man is clean but does not come to observe it at its appointed time, to bring an offering acceptable before the Lord and to eat and drink before the Lord on the day of his festival, that man, though clean and nearby, shall be cut off, because he did not bring the Lord’s offering at its appointed time. That man shall bear his own sin.

So that the Israelites would come and celebrate the Passover on its appointed day, the fourteenth day of the first month, between the evenings, from the third part of the day until the third part of the night; for two parts of the day were allotted to daylight, and the third to evening.
This is what the Lord commanded you to observe between the evenings.

It must not be slaughtered at any time during daylight, but only at the boundary of evening. They shall eat it in the evening until a third of the night has passed. Whatever remains of any of its meat after a third of the night has passed shall be burned with fire.
They must not boil it in water or eat it raw, but roasted over a fire, cooked over a fire by roasting, with its head, its internal organs, and its legs.
For this reason the Lord commanded the children of Israel to observe the Passover on its appointed day.

You too must command the children of Israel to observe the Passover throughout their days, every year, once a year on its appointed day. It shall come before the Lord as an acceptable remembrance, and no plague to kill or strike them shall come upon them in that year when they observe the Passover at its appointed time, in every respect as commanded.
It must not, therefore, be eaten outside the Lord’s sanctuary, but in front of the Lord’s sanctuary. All the people of the congregation of Israel shall observe it at its appointed time.

Everyone who comes on its appointed day, from twenty years old and upward, shall eat it in the sanctuary of your God, before the Lord. For it is written and ordained in this way that they shall eat it in the Lord’s sanctuary.

And when the children of Israel enter the land that they will possess, the land of Canaan, they shall set up the Lord’s tabernacle in the middle of the land, among one of their tribal divisions, until the Lord’s sanctuary is built in the land.

And in the days when a house has been built in the Lord’s name in the land of their inheritance, they shall go there and slaughter the Passover in the evening, as the sun is setting, during the third part of the day.

They shall bring its blood up to the base of the altar and place its fat on the fire upon the altar. They shall eat its meat roasted over a fire within the courtyard of the sanctuary dedicated to the Lord’s name.

They may not observe the Passover in their towns or in any other places, except before the Lord’s tabernacle, or before the house where his name dwells within it. They must not stray from following the Lord.

And you, Moses, command the children of Israel to observe the ordinance of the Passover, as you were commanded to tell them, year by year, on its appointed days, and the Festival of Unleavened Bread. They are to eat unleavened bread for seven days and celebrate its festival, bringing an offering each day during these seven days of rejoicing before the Lord, on the altar of your God. 23 For you celebrated this festival in haste when you came out of Egypt, until you crossed the sea into the wilderness of Shur, for you completed it on the shore of the sea.
After this I made known to you the law concerning the Sabbath days in the wilderness of Sin, which lies between Elim and Sinai.
I also told you about the land’s Sabbaths on Mount Sinai, and the jubilee years among the sabbatical years. But we have not told you its year until you enter the land that you will possess.
The land will also observe its Sabbaths while they live on it, and they will know the jubilee year.

For this reason I have established for you the weeks of years and the jubilees: forty-nine jubilees, one week of years, and two years from the days of Adam until this day. There are still forty years ahead for learning the Lord’s commandments, until they cross over into the land of Canaan, crossing the Jordan toward the west.

The jubilees will pass until Israel is cleansed of every offense of sexual immorality, impurity, defilement, sin, and error, and lives securely throughout the land. They will no longer have any Satan or any evil one, and the land will be clean from that time forever.
Now I have written for you the commandment concerning the Sabbaths and all the provisions of its laws.

For six days you shall work, but the seventh day is the Sabbath of the Lord your God. On it you shall do no work—you, your children, your male servants, your female servants, all your livestock, or the foreigner who lives among you.

Anyone who does any work on it shall die. Every person who profanes this day, who sleeps with a woman, who speaks on it about doing work or setting out on a journey on it, or about any buying or selling, who draws water on it that he did not prepare for himself on the sixth day, or who picks up any load to carry it out of his tent or his house, shall die.
On the Sabbath you shall do no work that you have not prepared for yourselves on the sixth day, so that you may eat, drink, rest, refrain from all work on this day, and bless the Lord your God.

For great is the honor that the Lord gave Israel: to eat, drink, and be satisfied on this festival day, and to rest on it from all human work, except burning incense and bringing offerings and sacrifices before the Lord for the days and Sabbaths.

Only this work shall be done on the Sabbath days in the sanctuary of the Lord your God: making atonement for Israel with the regular daily offering, as a memorial pleasing before the Lord. He will accept them forever, day by day, as you were commanded.
And anyone who does work, travels on a journey, or cultivates a field, whether at home or in any other place—
Anyone who does any of these things on the Sabbath day must die. Here ends the account of the Divisions of the Days.
